pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
> 🔢 **Strand 1 — Number**
Counting, calculating and reasoning with numbers — the language of trade, science and everyday life.

> 🎯 **Content standard** (B9.1.1)
- B9.1.1.1 — Apply the understanding of place value in solving real-life problems involving integers of any size, rounding these to given decimal places and significant figures. B9.1.1.2 — Demonstrate understanding of the relationship between members of the rational number system and solve real-life problems involving union and intersection of sets.

> 🎯 **In this chapter you will learn to:**
- express integers and decimals to given numbers of significant figures and decimal places
- create and solve place-value puzzles and story problems, giving answers in standard form
- describe the real number system — natural numbers, whole numbers, integers, rational and irrational numbers — with a set diagram
- solve real-life problems involving union and intersection of two sets

pages.title: Significant figures and decimal places
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Express integers to a given number of significant figures and decimal places.
Curriculum indicator B9.1.1.1.1
## ✏️ Example 1.1
a) Express 857,386,321 to five, four and three significant figures. b) Write 98,745.9674 correct to three, two and one decimal place(s).
**Solution**
a) 5 s.f.: **857,390,000**; 4 s.f.: **857,400,000**; 3 s.f.: **857,000,000**
b) 3 d.p.: 98,745.967|4 → **98,745.967**; 2 d.p.: 98,745.96|74 → **98,745.97**; 1 d.p.: 98,745.9|674 → **98,746.0**

pages.title: Place value puzzles and story problems
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Use knowledge and understanding of place value to solve real-life problems.
Curriculum indicator B9.1.1.1.2
## ✏️ Example 1.2
I am a 6-digit number. My first digit is 5 more than my last digit, but 2 less than my second digit. My second digit is the third multiple of 3, while my fourth digit is the second multiple of 3. My third digit is the quotient when my fourth digit is divided by my last digit. My fourth and fifth digits are consecutive numbers (counting down). What number am I? Write it in standard form.
**Solution**
Work out the digits in a sensible order:
| **Digit** | **Reasoning** | **Value** |
|---|---|---|
| second | third multiple of 3 = 3 × 3 | 9 |
| fourth | second multiple of 3 = 2 × 3 | 6 |
| first | 2 less than the second: 9 − 2 | 7 |
| last (sixth) | first is 5 more than the last: 7 − 5 | 2 |
| third | fourth ÷ last = 6 ÷ 2 | 3 |
| fifth | consecutive with the fourth: 6 − 1 | 5 |
The number is **793,652 = 7.93652 × 10^{5}**
Check every clue: 7 = 2 + 5 ✓, 7 = 9 − 2 ✓, 9 = 3 × 3 ✓, 6 = 2 × 3 ✓, 3 = 6 ÷ 2 ✓, 6 and 5 consecutive ✓.
> 🧪 **Activity 1.1 — Make your own puzzle**
Write a similar "Who am I?" place-value puzzle for a 5- or 6-digit number. Exchange puzzles with a partner, solve them and write each answer in standard form. Check that your clues lead to only **one** answer.

pages.title: Exercise 1.2
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Exercise 1.2** — try these on paper or in your head, then tap **Quick check** to see the answers.
1. I am a 5-digit number. My ten-thousands digit is the smallest odd prime. My thousands digit is twice my ten-thousands digit. My hundreds digit is the sum of the first two digits. My tens digit is 0 and my ones digit is one less than my hundreds digit. Who am I?
2. A country exported 3,450,600 bags of cocoa one year and 2.98 × 10^{6} bags the next. Find the total in standard form correct to 3 significant figures.

pages.title: The real number system
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Solve problems on the relationship between members of the rational number system using union and intersection of sets.
Curriculum indicator B9.1.1.2.1
| **Set** | **Symbol** | **Description** | **Examples** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Natural (counting) numbers | N | {1, 2, 3, …} | 1, 25, 400 |
| Whole numbers | W | natural numbers and 0 | 0, 7, 99 |
| Integers | Z | whole numbers and their negatives | −5, 0, 12 |
| Rational numbers | Q | numbers that can be written as [[a/b]], a and b integers, b ≠ 0 (terminating or repeating decimals) | [[3/4]], −2, 0.6, 0.333… |
| Irrational numbers | Q′ | numbers that cannot be written as a fraction (non-terminating, non-repeating decimals) | √2, √5, π |
| Real numbers | R | all rational and irrational numbers | every point on the number line |
[[fig:m9-f02|Figure 1.1: The real number system: N ⊂ W ⊂ Z ⊂ Q, and Q ∪ Q′ = R]]
> 🔑 **Key idea: Subset** — Set A is a **subset** of B (A ⊂ B) if every element of A is also in B. N ⊂ W ⊂ Z ⊂ Q ⊂ R. Rational and irrational numbers have no elements in common: Q ∩ Q′ = { }.
## ✏️ Example 1.3
Write the factors of 12 and 15 and represent them on a Venn diagram. Find F₁₂ ∩ F₁₅ and F₁₂ ∪ F₁₅.
**Solution**
F₁₂ = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12} F₁₅ = {1, 3, 5, 15}
[[fig:m9-f03]]
Figure 1.2: Factors of 12 and 15
F₁₂ ∩ F₁₅ = **{1, 3}** F₁₂ ∪ F₁₅ = **{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 12, 15}**

pages.title: Exercise 1.3
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Exercise 1.3** — try these on paper or in your head, then tap **Quick check** to see the answers.
1. To which of the sets N, W, Z, Q, Q′ does each number belong? a) −7 b) 0 c) [[5/8]] d) √9 e) √7 f) 0.121212… g) π
2. Is every integer a rational number? Is every rational number an integer? Explain with examples.
3. A = {multiples of 4 less than 30}, B = {multiples of 6 less than 30}. Draw a Venn diagram and list A ∩ B and A ∪ B.

parts.a: Yes: every integer n = [[n/1]]. No: [[1/2]] is rational but not an integer.

pages.title: Real-life problems on sets
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Apply the concept of sets to solve problems on the relationship between members of the rational number system and solve real-life problems involving union and intersection of two sets.
Curriculum indicator B9.1.1.2.2
## ✏️ Example 1.4
There are 80 farmers in a village who grow maize or beans. Fifty of them grow beans and sixty grow maize. Every farmer grows at least one crop. Represent the information on a Venn diagram and find the number of farmers who grow a) both crops b) only one crop.
**Solution**
[[fig:m9-f04]]
Figure 1.3: Farmers growing beans and maize
Let x grow both. Then 50 − x grow beans only and 60 − x grow maize only.
(50 − x) + x + (60 − x) = 80 ⟹ 110 − x = 80 ⟹ x = 30
a) **30 farmers** grow both. b) Beans only 20 + maize only 30 = **50 farmers** grow only one crop.
## ✏️ Example 1.5
In a class of 42 learners, 25 study French, 20 study Ewe and 8 study neither. How many study both?
**Solution**
n(F ∪ E) = 42 − 8 = 34. Using n(F ∪ E) = n(F) + n(E) − n(F ∩ E):
34 = 25 + 20 − n(F ∩ E) ⟹ n(F ∩ E) = **11 learners**

pages.title: Exercise 1.4
pages.body:

1. In a survey of 100 households, 72 have a radio, 58 have a television and 5 have neither. How many have both?
2. Of 60 traders, 38 sell rice and 30 sell beans; 10 sell both. How many sell neither?

pages.title: Chapter 1 summary
pages.body:
- Round to significant figures from the first non-zero digit; to decimal places after the point.
- N ⊂ W ⊂ Z ⊂ Q; rational and irrational numbers together make the real numbers.
- n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).
